section.title: Introduction
section.para: A glossary maps surface forms, including multiword terms, to stable identifiers. The package opennlp.tools.glossary compiles a list of GlossaryEntry values into an AhoCorasickGlossaryMatcher and mounts that matcher on the document pipeline through GlossaryAnnotator. Every hit is a span over the original text, so consumers read identifiers and covered text without re-tokenizing.

section.title: Matching through a pipeline
section.para: The annotator requires no other layer, so it can sit anywhere in a DocumentAnalyzer. The example below builds a three-entry glossary, runs it after a model-free tokenizer, and reads GlossaryAnnotator.GLOSSARY back with exact spans. Case-insensitive matching is on, so a registered lowercase term still covers a mixed-case mention while the span points at the original characters. GlossaryUsageExampleTest asserts the behavior shown here.
A document that never saw a glossary annotator reads as an empty glossary layer, and the key is absent from layers().

section.title: Matching with an offset-aware normalizer
section.para: The two-argument matcher compares characters literally, aside from the optional per-code-point case fold. Length-changing orthographic folds such as German umlaut expansion, full Unicode case folding, whitespace collapse, or dash folding are supplied through the three-argument constructor that takes a non-null OffsetAwareNormalizer. Terms and text are folded before the automaton runs, and every hit span is mapped back to the original text. Stemming and lemmatization are not expressible this way. GlossaryUsageExampleTest mirrors the example below.

section.title: Matching inflected forms through TermAnalyzer
section.para: Token-level inflection needs a stemmer. Build a TermAnalyzingGlossaryMatcher over a TermAnalyzer that case-folds and stems. The matcher runs Aho-Corasick over normalized tokens and reports spans from the first matched token's original start to the last matched token's original end, so a registered hot dog covers the surface hot dogs. Keep AhoCorasickGlossaryMatcher for exact and orthographic matching when no tokenizer is required. GlossaryUsageExampleTest mirrors the example below; TermAnalyzingGlossaryMatcherTest pins the reproduction.

The word tokenizer drops punctuation, so the characters between consecutive tokens do not take part in matching: hot-dogs, hot, dogs, and even the sentence-crossing hot. Dogs all match a registered hot dog, with the span covering the separators between the matched tokens. Matching hyphenated compounds is intentional; run sentence-sized inputs when a hit must not cross a sentence boundary. A lemmatizing analyzer is rejected at construction, because lemmas need part-of-speech tags that plain text cannot supply.

section.title: Combining matchers with CompositeGlossaryMatcher
section.para: A document can only carry one glossary layer, so a pipeline that wants both exact and inflected hits combines the matchers behind a single GlossaryAnnotator with a CompositeGlossaryMatcher. Delegates are consulted in the order given and earlier matchers win: a hit survives only when its span overlaps no hit already accepted from an earlier matcher. Register the exact matcher first and the inflected matcher second, and the inflected path fills only the gaps the exact automaton misses. Merged hits come back in text order. GlossaryUsageExampleTest mirrors the example below; CompositeGlossaryMatcherTest pins the merge rules.
